strengths: Novel and clearly stated central contribution: the first demonstration that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between model soup ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs — including different SSL objectives (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), not merely different hyperparameters. This genuinely expands the known cases where souping works (Fig. 2, §4.1).

Careful and fair baseline design: the authors construct a 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline with equal search cost (Fig. 3), so gains are not simply attributable to extra compute; supervised soups and TTA (SAR) are also compared (Tab. 3).

Extensive evaluation: ImageNet plus 7 shifted test sets, VTAB across 21 tasks × 16 corruption conditions (336 test sets), disjoint vs. joint splits to quantify the effect of using test-distribution data, and a second stock (Franca) to probe generality (Fig. 4).

The strongest results (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) are cleanly attributed: inter-training on the shifted distribution rather than the test samples themselves delivers most of the gain, and the disjoint-split controls make this credible.

Self-Seasoning is a sensible label-free extension of seasoning (kNN-entropy minimization over mixture coefficients) with released PyTorch code (Appendix D), and the paper is honest that supervised seasoning still beats it overall (Tab. 5).

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: hyperparameters, schedules, and implementation details are provided in Appendix B, and the mini-VTAB-C benchmark is shared. The limitations section is candid about modest gains and the need for unlabeled shifted data.
weaknesses: Many headline gains are small: on VTAB the Self-Soup advantage over the continued SSL + supervised soup baseline is ~0.3–1% mean accuracy (Tab. 4), and on ImageNet the IN-Val gain is negative for uniform mixing (79.11 vs 79.23, Tab. 1). No error bars or statistical significance are reported for any comparison, so it is hard to judge robustness of ≲1% differences.

The largest gains (+3.5%, +7%) require unlabeled data from the corrupted test distribution — essentially transductive/domain-adaptation access that will often be unavailable, as the authors themselves concede. The more practically relevant in-distribution gains are much smaller.

Scale and generality are limited: experiments are at ViT-B with mostly one stock (MAE); the second stock (Franca) is tested only with pairwise MAE–MoCoV3 mixes. Fine-tuning is only 10 epochs, and it is unclear whether gains persist with longer or stronger fine-tuning recipes.

Compute cost of the method is discussed only qualitatively. Inter-training multiple models (e.g., 4 × 100K steps on ImageNet-C) plus N fine-tunings per inter-training is expensive; a quantitative cost accounting versus the accuracy gains would strengthen the deployment-cost argument.

The formalization (Eq. 2) is largely notational — the framework is 'any soup whose ingredients differ in SSL runs' — so the paper's methodological contribution rests almost entirely on its empirical findings, and the space of design choices explored (3 SSL algorithms, arbitrary hyperparameters) is acknowledged to be a small slice.

Results are mixed across corruption families (worse on noise by -1%, Tab. 4b), and Self-Seasoning underperforms substantially on several structured tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 34.6, dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs 11.6), which tempers the claim that label-free mixing is broadly 'competitive.'

strengths: Genuinely novel contribution: the paper is the first to show that linear mode connectivity and productive souping can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs (different SSL algorithms, hyperparameters, and data), which meaningfully expands the model-soup literature beyond supervised settings (Figs. 2, 5).

Comprehensive and well-controlled evaluation: eight ImageNet test sets (including ReaL, V2, A, R, C, LAION-C), 21 VTAB tasks across 336 test conditions (clean + 15 corruptions), a second stock (Franca ViT-B), and augmentation-variant ablations (Tabs. 6-7) support the generality of the findings.

Fair and thoughtful baselines: the authors construct a 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline with equal search/development cost, include an ensemble comparison (even though it is more expensive at inference), and compare directly against Model Ratatouille (Tab. 5) — showing Self-Soups match it without auxiliary labeled datasets.

The §4.3 experiment is well designed: inter-training on even-indexed test samples and evaluating on odd-indexed samples (disjoint setting) cleanly demonstrates shift-aware robustness gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) without training on the actual test samples, and comparison against SAR test-time adaptation contextualizes the results.

Self-Seasoning is a sensible unsupervised extension: learning mixture coefficients by minimizing kNN entropy (Eq. 3) is controlled against labeled seasoning using identical ingredients and parameters, and the full PyTorch implementation is provided in the supplement.
Honest limitations discussion (§6) acknowledges that the largest gains require unlabeled shifted data, that other gains are modest, and that only 3 of many SSL families are studied.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are modest outside the corruption settings: on IN-Val, best Self-Soup results (e.g., Uniform Mix 79.09 vs. 79.12 for supervised soup in Tab. 1) are within noise of or slightly below supervised soups, and some cells (e.g., IN-HR Best Ingredient 87.28 vs. 87.34) regress. Headline claims rest mainly on ImageNet-C/LAION-C. No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, despite many reported differences of <0.3%.

The +7% LAION-C and +3.5% IN-C gains depend on access to unlabeled data from the test/shift distribution, which is a strong practical assumption. The paper does address this honestly and compares to TTA, but the applicability of the largest gains is narrow relative to how prominently they are presented.

Short inter-training runs (5 epochs for the main souping experiment, §4.1) leave open whether LMC across diverse SSL algorithms persists at realistic pre-training scales; the evidence is limited to ViT-B with brief continued training.

Reproducibility gaps in the manuscript itself: the abstract's code URL is truncated ('https://github.com/'), and Section D ('Data and Code') in the supplement is entirely empty. This directly undercuts the paper's reproducibility claim at submission time.

Several typos and inconsistencies undermine polish: 'varing' (§4.5), 'Experments' (Appendix A), self-referential Table 7 caption ('same experiment setup as Tab. 7'), and the fine-tuning learning rates in §4.5 ({6e-8, 8e-8, 1e-4, 1.5e-4}) span an implausible range and appear to contain an error.

Fig. 2 heatmaps are difficult to read (axis labeling of 4 ingredients on 2D axes, and the claim that 'the worst models are always the ingredients alone' is not verifiable from the color scales without more precise reporting); tabulated values for the mixture grid would strengthen the LMC claim.

Section 4.6's claim that 'seasoning can outperform fine-tuning' is supported only for very low sample counts (<500) and only for natural tasks; the fine-tuning baseline dominates elsewhere (Tab. 9), which should be stated more prominently in the main text.
